nhiip-india-corridor-land-acquisition.confidence_note: The link between this loan and the harm rests on four documents and is stated here so it can be attacked. First, the Bank’s procurement plan for this project of 9 June 2020 carries the Birpur-Bihpur km 0 to 106 section of NH-106 as a works package against loan IBRD-83010, under the Bank’s prior review, with an actual contract amount of US$101,671,942.50; its 2013 predecessor carries the same works at Rs 435.89 crore as package 12 with a resettlement-plan implementation agency alongside. Second, the ministry’s resettlement action plan for that package, disclosed by the Bank in February 2014, names Manikpur in Madhepura at km 75+400 to 76+000 among the villages on it. Third, the Patna High Court in its own suo motu proceeding calls the works the construction of NH-106 Birpur-Bihpur for 106 kilometres under Phase-I of NHIIP. Fourth, the compensation case arising on that road names the Land Acquisition Officer cum Competent Authority, N.H.-106 and the Nodal Officer, NHIIP as respondents. No court record gives a loan or credit number; the loan number comes from the Bank’s own procurement plan, and the match between the court’s Rs 675 crore IL&FS contract and the plan’s US$101,671,942.50 is a correspondence at the exchange rate of the year of award, not something a document states. The works were not paid for by a different operation. The transfer of the unfinished works to the Green National Highways Corridor Project was approved on 6 July 2022, by that project’s first restructuring, which took in the balance NHIIP civil works contracts for 155 km and created new components funded with US$95.41 million reallocated from its own; it did not happen at NHIIP’s closing in 2020. Six Green Corridors procurement plans, from December 2020 to March 2025, were searched and none names NH-106, Birpur or Bihpur; the only trace is a technical audit consultancy covering stretches under both projects. So the NH-106 works sat inside loan IBRD-83010 under prior review until the loan closed, and nothing found shows them paid from the Green Corridors loan afterwards. What no document establishes. Smt. Nutan’s parcel is not tied to a chainage anywhere: the match is her village, which the loan’s resettlement plan places on the financed package, and the acquiring authority, not her plot number. She is not in that plan’s 2014 list of affected owners for Manikpur, which names other people; a Nutan Devi recorded in the same plan as a residential squatter at km 9+450 in Bhagwanpur, Supaul is a different person. Whether she is entitled to Rs 3,66,61,312 is open: the execution order was set aside on 17 November 2025 and the state’s challenge to the award is pending. The two other Patna High Court compensation claims on this road — Rajeev Kumar Mishra for five katha at Tola Kamalpur in Supaul, a village the resettlement plan also names, at km 43+000 to 44+400, whose writ of 2016 was sent to a civil court undecided after nine years on 15 September 2025, and Vijay Kumar for 0.1990 acre at Madanpur, Madhepura valued as residential rather than commercial, taken up on 14 July 2026 — are pleadings the courts have not ruled on, and are recorded here as pleadings. None of the project-wide figures — 775 acres, 558 acres private, 6,390 structures, 11,138 project-affected people, 347 grievances — is confirmed by anything outside the Bank, and nothing found gives a count of people relocated, contradicts the zero in the killed field, or says how many owners on this corridor went unpaid. A Lok Sabha speech of 17 March 2020 that says farmers’ land for NH-106 was acquired with no money to pay compensation is about km 124 to 136, the Kosi missing link in Package II, which this loan did not finance, and is not evidence for this card. The only Indian state audit found, the Principal Director of Audit’s report and certificate on loan 8301-IN for 2018-19 dated 6 March 2020, is unqualified and says nothing about land.

field_changes.community: The completion report of 29 June 2022 gives the scale: "The project impacted 775 acres of land, including 558 acres of private land, 6390 structures (including 451 CPRs) and 11,138 PAPs", CPRs being common property resources and PAPs project-affected people. It says that at closure compensation and eligible assistance were duly paid to all project-affected people in six of the eleven road corridors, and that the remaining five roads, in Bihar and West Bengal, were transferred to another Bank-funded project, the Green National Highways Corridor Project. The Independent Evaluation Group’s review of 21 February 2023 records that disbursement of compensation "were substantially delayed in several sections", while saying that by closing all 11,138 people had been compensated for the subprojects completed under the project — the same six of eleven corridors, so the delay carries no length, no date and no number of people. Both documents record that the land acquisition was mis-sized: poor road designs led to inaccurate assessments of how much land was needed, particularly on four roads in Bihar, and to variations in the numbers of those affected. The completion report says that although each state public works department had guaranteed land availability before the works began, in practice the entire land was not handed over. It rates social safeguards performance Moderately Satisfactory. The project received 347 grievances and the report says all but one were resolved. Neither document gives a count of people relocated, neither uses the words displaced or relocated, and neither names a village. One of the five Bihar and West Bengal roads can be named from documents outside those two reports, and it is the corridor on which the record of unpaid compensation sits. The road is NH-106 between Birpur and Bihpur. The Bank’s own procurement record puts it inside this loan twice. The Procurement Plan for Phase I of NHIIP of 24 September 2013 lists the rehabilitation and upgrading of the Birpur-Bihpur section of NH 106 as works package 12, Rs 435.89 crore, international competitive bidding with prequalification, reserved for the Bank’s prior review, with bid opening expected on 7 March 2014, and separately lists a consultant or non-governmental organisation to implement the resettlement action plan for the same section. The project’s procurement plan of 9 June 2020, three and a half months before the loan closed, carries the same works as package NHIIP-BR-106-7 against loan IBRD-83010, under the Road Improvement and Maintenance Component, subject to prior review, with an actual contract amount of US$101,671,942.50 and the status Under Implementation; an Authority Engineer consultancy for the same section, NHIIP-BR-106-AE-07, sits on the same plan against the same loan number. The acquisition on this road was planned under the loan as well: the ministry’s Social Impact Assessment and Resettlement Action Plan of February 2014, disclosed by the Bank as RP1245 v11, covers Package I of the road, Birpur to Udakishanganj, km 0 to km 106, and counts 1,997 project-affected people, 449 affected households of which 140 lost land and 309 lost structures, 17 common property resources, 9.2491 hectares of private land to be acquired in Supaul district and 7.3245 hectares in Madhepura, and a resettlement budget of Rs 76.49 crore. It names the villages the road passes through with their chainages, Manikpur in Madhepura district at km 75+400 to 76+000 among them, and lists 39,083 square metres of land at Manikpur valued at Rs 1,95,41,500. What the Indian courts record on that road is this. The Patna High Court has run a suo motu proceeding on the construction since 2019 (CWJC 320 of 2019). On 24 January 2023 the Chief Justice recorded that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways had contracted the work to IL&FS Engineering and Construction Company Limited by an agreement of 29 July 2016, commencement 3 October 2016, completion due 2 October 2019, contract value Rs 675 crore; that the work was divided into three sections over km 0 to km 106; that the court had already recorded inordinate delay; and that beyond the hindrances the contractor had named there were at least 507 electric poles to be moved and "at least 60 structures (house, building, shops and religious structures)" still to be removed before the site could be handed over. That is the court, in its own voice, recording sixty households, shops and places of worship standing on the alignment of a loan-financed package six years after the works began. On 18 April 2025 the Acting Chief Justice recorded that the contractor had undertaken the work of NH-106 Birpur-Bihpur for 106 kilometres under Phase-I of NHIIP, that it was due to finish on 2 October 2019, that "only 95.31% of the work has been completed", and that in the absence of link roads or diversions even the 103 kilometres built was not being put to use, which he described as creating protest among people living nearby and regular commuters. The compensation record runs through one landowner’s case, Smt. Nutan of Ward No. 2, Manikpur, Madhepura, and it is the only instance in which an Indian court has acted on non-payment on this corridor rather than recited it. Her land was acquired under the National Highways Act; the Land Acquisition Officer cum Competent Authority, N.H.-106, Madhepura and the Project Director, N.H.-106 at Purnea are respondents in the High Court’s own cause title, and in a later writ so is the Nodal Officer, NHIIP, Road Construction Department, Bihar. The statutory arbitrator for a compensation dispute on a national highway is the Divisional Commissioner, and on 16 July 2021, in Arbitration Case 31 of 2020, the Commissioner of Koshi Division at Saharsa directed that the Collector of Madhepura take possession of her land only after the compensation had been calculated as that order required. On 28 March 2023, in CWJC 1694 of 2023, the High Court ordered the authorities to "maintain status quo with respect to the land of the petitioner" while the writ was pending; the petitioner’s case, which the court did not decide, was that the authorities had put the sum payable at Rs 3,66,61,312 in a letter of 4 April 2022 and were building without paying it. On 9 May 2023 the court sent her to the enforcement route under section 36 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The execution court, the Additional District Judge-III at Madhepura, disposed of Execution Case 06 of 2023 on 8 February 2024 by directing the Executive Engineer, National Highway, Madhepura to pay her Rs 3,66,61,312 within fifteen days. On 10 September 2024, in CWJC 13438 of 2024, the High Court disposed of a further writ by asking the execution court to secure compliance within eight weeks and directing counsel for the ministry and for the National Highways Authority of India to co-operate in complying with the order of 8 February 2024 — the court acting on a payment that had not been made, though it added the words "if the award holds the field till date". It did not hold. On 17 November 2025, in C.Misc. 919 of 2024, the Executive Engineer of the Madhepura National Highway Division won an order quashing the execution order of 8 February 2024 on the ground that an Additional District Judge was not the court competent to enforce an arbitral award of that value; the parties were sent to the District Judge of Madhepura sitting as a Commercial Court, and the state’s own Miscellaneous Appeal No. 1 of 2022 against the award is recorded as still pending there. That order is the court’s own recital of what it was quashing, and it is where the award of 16 July 2021 and the figure of Rs 3,66,61,312 are set down as facts rather than as a party’s account. More than four years after the award, the money has not been paid and the amount is still in dispute.
field_changes.conditions: The loan triggered the Bank's policy on involuntary resettlement (OP 4.12) and its policy on indigenous peoples (OP 4.10), the latter because six of the corridors, in Odisha, Rajasthan and West Bengal, ran through areas where indigenous communities live. Corridor-specific resettlement action plans were prepared under a resettlement policy framework and published in India and at the Bank's InfoShop. Indigenous peoples development plans were written and their actions folded into the resettlement plans. The project required contractors to be handed 80 per cent of the land free of encumbrance within a set period, and gave grievance redressal committees a role in deciding eligibility where the plan's figures and what was found on the ground differed. The resettlement plan for the Birpur-Bihpur package records that OP 4.10 was not triggered on that road, there being no village along it with a significant scheduled tribe population, so no separate indigenous peoples plan was prepared for it.

corrections: Round 40's check log and checked entry recorded a 'chainage inconsistency' across the records - km 0 to 106 in four documents, km 0.00 to 136.00 in the Mishra petition, and the Bank's assessment calling the stretch Birpur-Udakishanganj rather than Birpur-Bihpur. There is no inconsistency. The ministry's resettlement action plan of February 2014 says the Birpur-Bihpur section of NH-106 runs km 0 to km 136 and is split into two packages: Package I, Birpur to Udakishanganj, km 0 to km 106, and Package II, Udakishanganj to Bihpur, km 106 to km 136, the Kosi missing link. The loan financed Package I. Every figure in the records is right for the thing it describes.

The checker's recommended ground for promotion - that the Patna High Court 'records as fact, not as pleading' the award, the execution order, the fifteen days and the non-payment - is only partly right, and the strongest document for it is one neither round found. In CWJC 13438 of 2024 the award, the amount and the words 'till date, the petitioner has not been accorded the award amount' all sit inside the narrative of the petitioner's senior counsel. What the court does in its own voice is direct the execution court to secure compliance within eight weeks and direct the ministry's and the Highways Authority's counsel to co-operate, qualified by 'if the award holds the field till date'. The award of 16 July 2021 and the figure of Rs 3,66,61,312 are set down as the court's own recital of the orders under challenge in C.Misc. 919 of 2024, order of 17 November 2025.

A card promoted on the execution order of 8 February 2024 without reading forward would have been wrong within fourteen months. On 17 November 2025 the Patna High Court set that order aside, on the application of the Executive Engineer of the Madhepura National Highway Division, on the ground that an Additional District Judge was not the court competent to enforce an arbitral award of that value, and sent the parties to the District Judge of Madhepura as Commercial Court. The state's Miscellaneous Appeal No. 1 of 2022 against the award is recorded as pending there. The compensation is still unpaid; the amount is no longer settled.

The financing link is firmer than the 2013 procurement plan the checker found. The project's own procurement plan of 9 June 2020 carries the Birpur-Bihpur km 0 to 106 works as package NHIIP-BR-106-7 against loan IBRD-83010 - the loan number on this card - under the Road Improvement and Maintenance Component, subject to the Bank's prior review, with an actual contract amount of US$101,671,942.50 and the status Under Implementation, with an Authority Engineer consultancy for the same section on the same plan against the same loan. The checker's caveat that no document names the loan number is withdrawn as to the Bank's own records; it still holds for the court records.

The transfer to the Green National Highways Corridor Project did not happen in 2020. That project's completion report of 11 September 2026 records that its first restructuring, approved 6 July 2022, incorporated the unfinished NHIIP activities - 'the balance NHIIP civil works contracts for 155 km' - and that US$95.41 million was reallocated from its own components to new Components D, E and F to finance them. The NHIIP restructuring paper of 30 September 2020 names no road and only says ongoing activities will be transferred. So for the whole period of this loan the NH-106 works sat in loan IBRD-83010 under prior review.

No Green Corridors procurement plan names NH-106. Six were read - 3 December 2020, 3 November 2021, 12 April 2022, 21 November 2023, 9 October 2024 and 20 March 2025 - and none contains Birpur, Bihpur or NH-106; the only trace is a technical audit consultancy for 'stretches under GNHCP & NHIIP'. The map's precedent that a link fails when a different operation paid for the works - the Burkina airport platform, the Sao Paulo Line 5 drop - therefore does not apply here.

The Green Corridors completion report says NHIIP 'closed in September 2022'. This project's own completion report, its restructuring papers and this card say the closing date was 30 September 2020. The Bank's record contradicts itself on when its own loan closed.

The card's confidence note said there was no Inspection Panel complaint. The Panel received a Request for Inspection on 18 December 2015, followed by 28 more, from community members in East Godavari district naming this project and the Andhra Pradesh Road Sector Project, submitted on behalf of over eighty affected people and alleging displacement from the widening of NH-216. The Panel issued a Notice of Non-Registration on 2 February 2016, having determined that neither project financed works on NH-216. So a complaint naming this project exists and was refused registration; no registered complaint about this project's own harm was found.

The acquisition on the harmed corridor was planned under this loan, and the claimants' villages are in the loan's own resettlement document. The ministry's Social Impact Assessment and Resettlement Action Plan for Package I, disclosed by the Bank as RP1245 v11 in February 2014, lists the villages along km 0 to 106 with their chainages. Manikpur in Madhepura district, where Smt. Nutan lives, is at km 75+400 to 76+000, and the plan's land schedule values 39,083 square metres there at Rs 1,95,41,500. Kamalpur in Supaul, where Rajeev Kumar Mishra's five katha at Tola Kamalpur lies, is at km 43+000 to 44+400, and plot numbers at Tola Kamalpur appear in the plan's list of affected holdings. Neither claimant is named in that list, which is a 2014 census and names other owners.

A near miss worth naming so it is not used later. The resettlement plan's own census of affected people records a Nutan Devi as a residential squatter at km 9+450 in Bhagwanpur, Supaul. That is not Smt. Nutan, wife of Arun Kumar Gupta, of Ward No. 2, Manikpur, Madhepura, whose case this is.

A second near miss. A Lok Sabha speech of 17 March 2020 by the member for Madhepura says land for NH-106 was acquired from farmers and the ministry has no money to pay compensation - a precise statement of this card's harm, from outside the lender. It is about km 124 to 136, the Kosi missing link between Udakishanganj and Bihpur, under the Prime Minister's package, which is Package II and which this loan did not finance. It is recorded on the card as what it is and is not treated as support.

The project's resettlement plan for NH-106 records that OP 4.10 was not triggered on that road, no village along it having a significant scheduled tribe population and no separate indigenous peoples plan being prepared. The card's conditions field, which says OP 4.10 was triggered because six corridors ran through areas where indigenous communities live, is right for the project and should not be read as covering this corridor.

The 2013 procurement plan's own heading reads 'Procurement Plan for Phase I of NHIIP [P121885]'. That is a third project-number artefact alongside the P121100 in the environmental assessment's file name. The catalogue record for the assessment carries P121185, which a query on the documents API for the word Birpur returns as the sole hit; the project is P121185 and the other two strings are typographical.
All eight World Bank URLs in the round 40 entry point at documents.worldbank.org, which does not serve. The same paths on documents1.worldbank.org serve, and the sources added here use that host.
nhiip-india-corridor-land-acquisition.what_the_outside_source_settles: That the works which took the land were a package of this loan: the Bank's procurement plan of 9 June 2020 puts Birpur-Bihpur km 0 to 106 of NH-106 against loan IBRD-83010, prior review, US$101,671,942.50 actually contracted, under implementation three months before the loan closed, and the ministry's resettlement plan for that package, disclosed by the Bank in 2014, names the villages along it. That the Patna High Court calls those works the construction of NH-106 Birpur-Bihpur under Phase-I of NHIIP, and records in its own voice that they were due to finish on 2 October 2019, that at least 60 houses, shops and religious structures were still standing on the alignment in January 2023, and that 95.31 per cent of the work was done by April 2025 with the 103 kilometres built unusable for want of link roads. That on that corridor the statutory arbitrator made an award on 16 July 2021 in favour of a landowner in a village the loan's own resettlement plan places at km 75+400, that an execution court ordered Rs 3,66,61,312 paid to her within fifteen days on 8 February 2024, that the High Court was still pressing for compliance in September 2024 with the project's own Nodal Officer, NHIIP among the respondents, and that the money had still not been paid when the state got the execution order quashed in November 2025. That the state is resisting the award rather than paying it. And that the works were not paid for by another operation: the transfer to the Green National Highways Corridor Project was approved on 6 July 2022, and no Green Corridors procurement plan names this road.
nhiip-india-corridor-land-acquisition.what_it_does_not_settle: The size of the harm. Every project-wide figure on this card remains the Bank's own, and the outside record holds one landowner's unpaid award and sixty unremoved structures, with no count of how many owners on this corridor went unpaid or how many people were moved. Whether Smt. Nutan's plot is on the financed 106 kilometres: her village is, by the loan's own resettlement plan, but no document places her holding on a chainage, and she is not in that plan's 2014 list of affected owners. Whether she is owed Rs 3,66,61,312: the execution order was set aside on 17 November 2025 and the state's appeal against the award is pending. Whether the works on her land were done before or after the loan closed on 30 September 2020. The two other Patna High Court compensation claims, Mishra and Vijay Kumar, which remain pleadings no court has ruled on. And nothing found bears on the zero in the killed field.
